payload.title: Methane, ammonia and water: selected molecular geometry

model.title: Methane, ammonia and water: selected molecular geometry
model.description: Unqualified proposal for human review: selectable normalized molecular coordinates, schematic lone pairs and an ideal tetrahedral guide. Geometry is prescribed, not predicted.
assumptions: Molecule input allows only discrete values 0=methane, 1=ammonia, 2=water; illustrative default 0.
Overlay inputs allow only 0=hidden or 1=shown; both have illustrative default 1.
Representative fixed H–central–H angles are approximately 109.47 degrees for methane, 107 degrees for ammonia and 104.5 degrees for water.
Coordinates are dimensionless normalized positions, not physical bond lengths. Every central-atom–hydrogen distance is one.
The central atom is at (0,0,0). Positive z points toward domain 4; x and y span the perpendicular plane.
Domain 1 is at (domain_1_x,0,domain_lower_z); domain 2 at (domains_23_x,domain_2_y,domain_lower_z); domain 3 at (domains_23_x,domain_3_y,domain_lower_z); domain 4 at (0,0,1).
Hydrogens occupy domains 1–4 for methane, 1–3 for ammonia and 1–2 for water. Remaining domains locate schematic lone-pair regions.

The ideal guide has domain 1 at (guide_radius,0,guide_z), domain 2 at (guide_domains_23_x,guide_domain_2_y,guide_z), domain 3 at (guide_domains_23_x,guide_domain_3_y,guide_z), and domain 4 at (0,0,1).
The guide represents ideal four-domain topology, not exact lone-pair directions. Molecular coordinates include prescribed bond-angle compression.
VSEPR qualitatively attributes compression to greater spatial demand of lone pairs than bonding pairs; the supplied numerical angles are independent of that explanation.
Atom identity, labels, bonds, occupancy and explanations all use the same molecule selector. Overlay toggles do not change atom geometry.
All normalized coordinates lie within [-1,1]; occupancy and visibility flags lie within [0,1]; domain counts lie within [0,4]. All square roots are strictly positive and the sole divisor is 1.5.
limitations: No quantum electron distributions, energies, geometry optimization or first-principles calculations are represented.
Lone-pair regions are schematic, not literal electron boundaries. Their direction and extent are not electron-density predictions.
Normalized equal bond lengths omit actual bond-length differences, atomic sizes, vibration, environment and molecular dynamics.
Representative angles display compression but do not calculate its magnitude or quantify repulsive forces.
This is a steady model: time_experiment=null. Camera rotation is inspection, not physical molecular motion. Existing mobile, keyboard, pause and reduced-motion controls remain unchanged.

snapshot.unfinished_question: What shape do methane, ammonia and water molecules take, and why?

definition.title: Methane, ammonia and water: shapes in 3D
definition.description: Select a molecule and rotate it to compare its atoms with its four electron domains. Methane is tetrahedral, ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, and water is bent.

limits: Geometry is prescribed, not predicted; VSEPR supplies a qualitative explanation, not a force calculation.
No quantum electron distributions, energies, geometry optimization or first-principles calculations are represented.
Lone-pair regions are schematic, not literal electron boundaries or predicted electron densities.
Equal normalized bond lengths omit actual bond-length differences, atomic sizes, vibration, environment and molecular dynamics.
Representative angles are approximately 109.47°, 107° and 104.5°; their compression is supplied, not calculated from repulsion.
The ideal tetrahedral guide shows four-domain topology, not exact lone-pair directions.
One normalized coordinate unit maps uniformly to 3 scene units on all axes. Model coordinates and equations remain unchanged; sizes of atoms and overlays are illustrative.

Discrete selections are 0=methane, 1=ammonia and 2=water; overlay toggles accept only 0 or 1. Labels, occupancy and geometry must follow the same selector; toggles do not alter molecular geometry. All three selections have four electron domains despite conservative independent interval bounds for the count node. Display bond_angle in degrees using the accepted conversion factor 57.29577951308232,

parts.label: Selected molecule
parts.explanation: Turn the model to see its shape from different sides. Turning the view does not mean the molecule is moving.

parts.label: Central atom: C, N or O
parts.explanation: The central atom is carbon in methane, nitrogen in ammonia, and oxygen in water.

parts.label: Bond 1
parts.explanation: This bond represents a shared pair of electrons between the central atom and hydrogen.

parts.label: Hydrogen 1
parts.explanation: This hydrogen is present in all three molecules. Its position helps show the bond angle.

parts.label: Bond 2
parts.explanation: This second shared electron pair forms another bond. Compare its direction with bond 1.

parts.label: Hydrogen 2
parts.explanation: This hydrogen is also present in every selection. The angle between its bond and bond 1 gets smaller from methane to water.

parts.label: Bond 3: methane or ammonia
parts.explanation: This bond is present in methane and ammonia. Water has a lone pair in this domain instead.

parts.label: Hydrogen 3: methane or ammonia
parts.explanation: This hydrogen appears in methane and ammonia, but not water.

parts.label: Bond 4: methane only
parts.explanation: Methane has a fourth bond. Ammonia and water have a lone pair in this domain instead.

parts.label: Hydrogen 4: methane only
parts.explanation: This fourth hydrogen completes methane's tetrahedral shape. A tetrahedron has four corners.

parts.label: Lone pair 3: water only
parts.explanation: A lone pair is a pair of electrons not shared in a bond. This schematic region appears only for water.

parts.label: Lone pair 4: ammonia or water
parts.explanation: This schematic region marks a lone pair in ammonia and water. Lone pairs need more room than bonding pairs in the VSEPR explanation.

parts.label: Ideal tetrahedral electron-domain guide
parts.explanation: The guide shows the ideal arrangement of four electron domains, meaning four regions around the central atom. Molecular shape names count atom positions, not lone pairs.

experiments.title: From methane to ammonia
experiments.prompt: Predict how the atom arrangement changes when you select ammonia. Select it, rotate the view, and compare the bonding-domain count.
experiments.explanation: Selecting ammonia hides hydrogen 4 and its bond, leaving a trigonal pyramid with three bonding domains and one lone pair. Coordinates are prescribed; view rotation is inspection only.

experiments.title: Why water is bent
experiments.prompt: Predict water's shape and lone-pair count. Select water and inspect the atoms separately from the schematic lone-pair regions.
experiments.explanation: Selecting water leaves two bonded hydrogens and two lone-pair domains. Atom positions define the bent molecular shape. VSEPR qualitatively explains compression; the displayed angle is supplied, not calculated from repulsion.

experiments.title: Four domains, different shapes
experiments.prompt: Predict whether methane has the same total electron-domain count as ammonia and water. Select methane and compare its atoms with the ideal guide.
experiments.explanation: Methane has four bonding domains and no lone pairs, giving a tetrahedral molecular shape. All three molecules have four electron domains, but molecular shape counts atom positions rather than lone pairs. The guide shows ideal topology, not exact lone-pair directions.

controls.help: Selects the molecule, changing atom identity, bonded hydrogens, schematic lone-pair occupancy and prescribed geometry together.
Shows or hides schematic lone-pair regions without changing atom positions or domain counts; these are not literal electron boundaries.
Shows or hides the ideal tetrahedral electron-domain guide without changing the selected molecule or its geometry.

coverage.explanation: Selection sets consistent atom occupancy and prescribed coordinates for tetrahedral methane, trigonal-pyramidal ammonia and bent water, alongside derived counts and selected angles. Geometry is represented, not predicted.

Selection changes bonded-atom and lone-pair occupancy together with their counts. Their sum remains four; molecular shape names describe atoms, while the optional ideal guide illustrates four-domain geometry.

VSEPR qualitatively relates greater lone-pair spatial demand to bond-angle compression. Schematic regions are not electron boundaries, and supplied angles do not calculate repulsive forces, energies or quantum electron distributions.

outcomes: Identify methane as tetrahedral, ammonia as trigonal pyramidal and water as bent.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular shape, which describes the positions of atoms.
Explain how bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom account for the different shapes using VSEPR.

generation_quality.scope: Recipe, label, connection and dependency checks only. Dependency paths do not prove numeric change. Overlap, recognizability, physical correctness and child usability require separate evaluation.

visual.scope: Eight fitted views; projected bounds, center-ray occlusion, conservative bounding-box overlaps and estimated two-line label capacity. These heuristics do not replace rendered-image or child usability review.

sampled_quality.scope: Defaults, five points per input plus presets, a midpoint context for apparently inactive controls, all-input endpoints, and lesson experiments. Finite geometry and observed changes only; no proof of scientific accuracy, recognizability or complete state-space coverage.
